b7cd800990751010.text: Read like a detective. When you need one fact fast, reading every word is the slow way. Good readers use three tricks. Skim to get the main idea. Look at the title, headings, pictures and the first line of each section. In ten seconds you know what the text is about. Scan to find one detail. Decide what you're hunting for — a time, a price, a name — and let your eyes jump until you see it. Numbers and bold words stand out. Search when the text is long. Use the website's search box, or press Ctrl + F (Cmd + F on a Mac) to find a word on the page. Texts are built to help you. Headings tell you what each part is about. Menus show a website's main sections. Tables put information in rows and columns, so you can run your finger across and down. Bold words and links jump out. When you think you've found it, check. Is it the right day? The right stop? The right size? A quick check saves a long walk.

dd8d0473527bb5fa.text: How little do people read?. Nielsen Norman Group is a company. It studies how people use websites. In 2008 it checked how long people spent on web pages. It also counted the words on each page. The average page had about 600 words. But people only had time to read about 28% of them. The researchers said 20% was more likely. The same group also used cameras that track where eyes look. People often read web pages in an F shape. They read across the top. Then across a bit lower down. Then down the left side. So good websites put the most important words first. They use headings, short paragraphs and lists. Think about it. About how much of a web page do people actually read? What is the F-pattern? How should a website be laid out if people scan it?

bf1cc0d4f5de1fee.text: How little do people read?. Nielsen Norman Group is a company that studies how people use websites. In 2008 it compared how long people spent on web pages with how many words those pages had. The average page had about 600 words, but people only had time to read about 28% of them. The researchers estimated 20% was more realistic, because some time goes on looking at layout and images. In eye-tracking research, the same group found people often scan web pages in an F-pattern: across the top, across a little lower, then down the left side. Designers use this — putting key words first, and using headings, short paragraphs and lists — so the page works for scanners. Think about it. About how much of a web page do people actually read? What is the F-pattern? How should a website be laid out if people scan it?
